fields.headline:
Unit 2
Motion in Two Dimensions
fields.subhead: Vectors, vector addition, and projectile motion — from first principles to real trajectories.

imageSubjects.hero: a basketball frozen mid-arc against a stormy sky

fields.headline:
2.1
Vectors & Vector Basics
fields.subhead: What a vector is, how to draw one, and how to describe its direction — before we add them together.

imageSubjects.section: a wooden protractor and ruler laid across graph paper

fields.headline: Three Words You Need First
fields.subhead: Write these before we go further.
fields.k1_b:
Has magnitude AND
direction.
Drawn as an arrow.
fields.k2_b:
The size or length.
Always positive.
fields.k3_b:
Which way it points.
Given as an angle.
fields.mustwrite: A vector needs both magnitude and direction — a number alone is not one.

imageSubjects.aside: a compass rose drawn in pencil on aged paper

fields.headline: How to Draw a Vector
fields.subhead: Every vector arrow carries two pieces of information at once.
fields.diagram: DIAGRAM TO HAND-BUILD: an arrow drawn from a starting point (tail) to an ending point (tip), arrow length measured against a scale, angle marked from a reference axis at the tail.
fields.a3_b:
Points the way
the vector acts.

fields.headline: Resolving a Vector Into Components
fields.subhead: Any vector can be broken into an x-part and a y-part using right-triangle trig.
fields.mustwrite: Components let you add vectors later — that's the whole point of resolving.

imageSubjects.concept: a drafting compass and protractor on a dark desk

fields.headline: Example: Resolving a Displacement
fields.subhead: We do this one together. Copy the setup, not just the answer.
fields.problem: A hiker walks 50 m at 30° above the horizontal. Find the x- and y-components.
fields.mustwrite: Ax = A cos(theta). Ay = A sin(theta). Always.

imageSubjects.aside: a hiking boot print in trail dust

fields.headline: Displacement, Worked
fields.subhead: Plug into both formulas — don't skip one.
fields.mustwrite: Check: Ax² + Ay² should equal A² again.

imageSubjects.data: a hand-drawn right triangle on graph paper

fields.headline: Degrees and Compass Directions
fields.subhead: The same vector can be described two ways — from an axis, or as a compass bearing.
fields.diagram: DIAGRAM TO HAND-BUILD: a compass rose (N/E/S/W) with a vector arrow drawn between two adjacent directions, showing the angle measured from each of the two nearby axes.
fields.a1_b:
Angle measured from
horizontal or vertical.

fields.headline: One Direction, Two Names
fields.subhead: "North of East" and "East of North" angles are always complementary — they add to 90°.
fields.keyq: Why do 40° North of East and 50° East of North point the exact same way?

imageSubjects.concept: a brass compass rose engraved on a dark surface

fields.headline: Example: Converting the Angle
fields.subhead: First rep — copy the reasoning, not just the number.
fields.problem: A vector points 40° North of East. Express this direction as an angle East of North.
fields.g2_b:
Same direction, as an
angle East of North
fields.mustwrite: North-of-East and East-of-North angles always add to 90°.

imageSubjects.aside: a protractor resting on a hand-drawn angle diagram

fields.headline: Converting the Angle, Worked
fields.subhead: Subtract from 90° — that's the whole method.
fields.f1_b:
East of North =
90° − North of East
fields.mustwrite: 40° North of East and 50° East of North are the same vector.

imageSubjects.data: two intersecting rulers forming a right angle

fields.headline: Your Turn: A Hiking Bearing
fields.subhead: Second rep — same method, different numbers.
fields.problem: A hiker walks at 65° East of North. Express this as an angle North of East.
fields.g2_b:
Same direction, as an
angle North of East
fields.mustwrite: Same rule: the two angles always add to 90°.

imageSubjects.aside: a topographic trail map with a pencil bearing line

fields.headline: Hiking Bearing, Worked
fields.subhead: Check yours against this before we move on.
fields.f1_b:
North of East =
90° − East of North
fields.mustwrite: 65° East of North and 25° North of East are the same vector.

imageSubjects.data: a compass sitting on a folded trail map

fields.headline: Quick Check: Resolve and Convert
fields.subhead: Both skills from this section, in one problem.
fields.problem: A force of 20 N acts at 70° East of North. Find its angle North of East.
fields.q2_b:
North of East =
90° − East of North

imageSubjects.setup: a small handheld dynamometer on a workbench

fields.headline:
Adding Vectors
Together
fields.subhead: Section 2.2 puts these skills to work — combining two vectors into one resultant.

imageSubjects.divider: two arrows converging toward a single point on a dark chalkboard

fields.headline:
2.2
Vector Addition
fields.subhead: Combine two vectors into a single resultant — first at 90°, then at any angle.

imageSubjects.section: two ropes pulling at right angles on a metal ring

fields.headline: Adding Perpendicular Vectors
fields.subhead: When two vectors meet at 90°, the Pythagorean theorem gives the resultant directly.
fields.diagram: DIAGRAM TO HAND-BUILD: two vectors drawn tip-to-tail at a right angle, with the resultant vector drawn as the hypotenuse connecting the start of the first to the tip of the second.
fields.a3_b:
Only when the vectors
are perpendicular.

fields.headline: Example: Plane in a Crosswind
fields.subhead: We do this one together. Copy the setup, not just the answer.
fields.problem: A plane flies 80 km/h east into a 20 km/h north crosswind. Find the resultant velocity.
fields.g1_b:
80 km/h, east
20 km/h, north
Perpendicular vectors
fields.mustwrite: Perpendicular vectors: R² = leg² + leg².

imageSubjects.aside: a small propeller plane silhouette against clouds

fields.headline: Plane in a Crosswind, Worked
fields.subhead: Write the direction, not just the number.
fields.work:
R = √(80²+20²) = 82.5 km/h
theta = arctan(20/80) = 14°
Direction: 14° N of E
fields.mustwrite: Always report both magnitude and direction together.

imageSubjects.data: an instrument panel compass and airspeed gauge

fields.headline: Adding Vectors at Any Angle
fields.subhead: When the angle isn't 90°, break each vector into components first.
fields.diagram: DIAGRAM TO HAND-BUILD: two vectors at an arbitrary angle to each other, each decomposed into dashed x- and y-component arrows, added separately, then recombined into a resultant vector.
fields.a1_b:
Break each vector
into x and y parts.
fields.a2_b:
Add the x's.
Add the y's.

fields.headline: Example: Two Forces on a Box
fields.subhead: Components first — this is not a Pythagorean-shortcut problem.
fields.problem: A 40 N force acts east, and a 30 N force acts 60° above east. Find the resultant force.
fields.mustwrite: Not perpendicular — resolve into components before adding.

imageSubjects.aside: two ropes pulling a wooden crate at different angles

fields.headline: Two Forces on a Box, Worked
fields.subhead: Add the x's, add the y's, then recombine.
fields.mustwrite: Add components on each axis separately, then recombine.

imageSubjects.data: a hand-drawn force diagram with two angled arrows

fields.headline: Your Turn: Two Displacements
fields.subhead: Same three steps. Work it, then check your answer.
fields.problem: Walk 30 m east, then 40 m at 45° above east. Find the resultant displacement.
fields.q2_b:
Add x's, add y's,
then R=√(x²+y²)

imageSubjects.setup: footprints in sand changing direction partway across a beach

fields.headline:
Projectile
Motion
fields.subhead: Section 2.3 puts vector addition to work — motion through the air, in three stages.

imageSubjects.divider: a basketball mid-arc against a dark gym backdrop

fields.headline:
2.3
Projectile Motion
fields.subhead: Model objects moving through the air under gravity alone — in three stages, from simplest to most complex.

imageSubjects.section: a ball frozen mid-arc against a stormy sky

fields.headline: Vocabulary You Need First
fields.subhead: Three words, used constantly for the rest of this section.
fields.k1_b:
An object moving
under gravity alone.
No other forces act.
fields.k2_b:
The curved path
the object follows.
A parabola.
fields.k3_b:
Total horizontal
distance travelled.
Launch point to landing.
fields.mustwrite: Horizontal and vertical motion happen independently — at the same time.

imageSubjects.aside: a stopwatch resting on a physics textbook

fields.headline: No Horizontal Force Needed
fields.subhead: Gravity acts only downward. Nothing pushes the object forward — horizontal velocity stays constant.
fields.keyq: If nothing pushes it forward, why does a thrown ball keep moving sideways?

imageSubjects.concept: a strobe-style multi-exposure photo of a thrown ball's arc

fields.headline:
Horizontal Launch
No Angle, No Height Change
fields.subhead: The simplest case: launched flat, lands at the same height it started.

imageSubjects.divider: a marble rolling off the edge of a dark table

fields.headline: The Flat Launch
fields.subhead: Horizontal velocity stays constant. Vertical motion is free fall from rest.
fields.diagram: DIAGRAM TO HAND-BUILD: object launched horizontally off a table edge, curving downward in a symmetric parabola. Mark equal horizontal spacing between time-steps (constant vx) and growing vertical spacing (accelerating vy).
fields.a1_b:
vx stays constant.
x = v0x · t
fields.a2_b:
Starts at rest (v0y=0).
y = ½ g t²
fields.a3_b:
Set y = launch height.
Solve for t.

fields.headline: Example: Rolling Off a Table
fields.subhead: We do this one together. Copy the setup, not just the answer.
fields.problem: A ball rolls off a 0.80 m table at 2.5 m/s. How long until it lands, and how far does it travel?
fields.mustwrite: Vertical motion decides the time. Horizontal motion decides the distance.

imageSubjects.aside: a marble resting at the edge of a wooden table

fields.headline: Table Roll-Off, Worked
fields.subhead: Solve vertical first — it gives you the time everything else depends on.
fields.mustwrite: Find time from the vertical drop, then use it for horizontal distance.

imageSubjects.data: a hand-drawn graph of height versus time

fields.headline: Your Turn: Off a Higher Shelf
fields.subhead: Same two steps. Work it, then check your answer.
fields.problem: A marble rolls off a 1.25 m shelf at 3.0 m/s. How far does it land from the shelf?
fields.q2_b:
y = ½ g t²
x = v0x · t

imageSubjects.setup: a bookshelf edge with a small marble balanced on it

fields.headline:
Adding a
Launch Angle
fields.subhead: Now the launch itself is angled — both velocity components exist from the start.

imageSubjects.divider: a soccer ball frozen mid-flight against floodlights

fields.headline: Launching at an Angle
fields.subhead: The initial velocity splits into a horizontal and a vertical part.
fields.diagram: DIAGRAM TO HAND-BUILD: object launched at an angle above level ground, arcing up to a peak then back down symmetrically to land at the same height. Show v0 decomposed into v0x and v0y at the launch point with a right-triangle construction.
fields.a1_b:
v0x = v0 cos(theta)
v0y = v0 sin(theta)

fields.headline: Example: A Kicked Soccer Ball
fields.subhead: Break the velocity into components before doing anything else.
fields.problem: A ball is kicked at 18 m/s at 30° above the ground. Find the time of flight and the range.
fields.mustwrite: Resolve v0 into v0x and v0y before solving anything else.

imageSubjects.aside: a soccer cleat mid-kick against a dark background

fields.headline: Kicked Ball, Worked
fields.subhead: Components first, then the two standard formulas.
fields.mustwrite: Time of flight depends only on v0y. Range depends on both.

imageSubjects.data: a hand-drawn parabolic arc sketch with labeled axes

fields.headline: Your Turn: A Launched Arrow
fields.subhead: Resolve first. Then apply the same two formulas.
fields.problem: An arrow is shot at 45 m/s at 40° above level ground. Find its range.

imageSubjects.setup: an archery target with an arrow mid-flight

fields.headline:
Height Changes
& Max Height
fields.subhead: Launch and landing points no longer match — and now we solve for the peak of the arc.

imageSubjects.divider: a cliffside overlook at dusk with a dark valley below

fields.headline: When Launch and Landing Differ
fields.subhead: The trajectory is no longer symmetric — the level-ground shortcut no longer applies.
fields.diagram: DIAGRAM TO HAND-BUILD: object launched at an angle from an elevated point, rising to a peak above the launch height, then descending past the launch height to land lower — an asymmetric arc, the descent longer than the ascent.
fields.a1_b:
At the peak, vy = 0.
t_apex = v0y / g
fields.a3_b:
Solve y(t)=y0+v0y t−½gt²
for total time.

fields.headline: Example: Max Height From a Cliff
fields.subhead: Find the peak first — everything else builds on it.
fields.problem: A rock is launched at 20 m/s at 35° from a 15 m cliff. Find the maximum height above the launch point.
fields.g1_b:
v0 = 20 m/s
theta = 35°
Launch height = 15 m
fields.g2_b:
Max height above
the launch point
fields.mustwrite: At maximum height, vertical velocity is exactly zero.

imageSubjects.aside: a rock resting on a cliff edge overlooking water

fields.headline: Max Height, Worked
fields.subhead: vy = 0 at the top — that's the condition that solves it.
fields.work:
Δy = 11.5²/(2×9.8) = 6.7 m
Peak height above ground: 21.7 m
fields.mustwrite: Report height above the launch point, and above the ground, separately.

imageSubjects.data: a hand-drawn height-versus-time curve peaking then falling

fields.headline: Example: Landing Below the Launch
fields.subhead: No shortcut formula here — solve the full position equation for time.
fields.problem: The same rock (20 m/s, 35°, from a 15 m cliff) lands on the ground below. Find the total time of flight.
fields.g1_b:
v0y = 11.5 m/s
Launch height = 15 m
Lands at height = 0
fields.mustwrite: y(t) = y0 + v0y t − ½ g t² — solve the quadratic for t.

imageSubjects.aside: a stopwatch beside a cliffside diagram sketch

fields.headline: Total Flight Time, Worked
fields.subhead: Quadratic formula — keep the positive root, it's the only one that makes sense.
fields.mustwrite: The negative root is a math artifact — time can't be negative.

imageSubjects.data: handwritten quadratic-formula work on notebook paper

fields.headline: Three Stages, One Idea
fields.subhead: Horizontal and vertical motion are always independent — only the setup changes.
fields.k2_b:
Add an angle.
Resolve v0 first.
fields.k3_b:
Add height change.
Solve for the peak or
the full quadratic.
fields.mustwrite: Every projectile problem: resolve v0, then work x and y separately.

imageSubjects.aside: three small sketched arcs of increasing complexity

fields.headline:
Vectors to
Projectile Motion
fields.subhead: Section 2.1 reviewed vectors, 2.2 added them together, and 2.3 put that skill to work predicting motion through the air.

imageSubjects.divider: a night sky with a single arcing firework trail
